_notice: FICTITIOUS program context. The definitions describe general US insurance terms in plain language for a support program that does not exist; they are not insurance or legal advice.
usage: Approved plain-language definitions a patient-services assistant may give when a patient asks what a term means. A definition explains the term in general; it never says how the patient's own plan applies it (that comes only from the verified case record).

terms.definition: A check with your insurance plan to find out how it covers a medicine, including whether approval is needed and what you may pay.
Approval your plan requires before it will cover a particular medicine. Your healthcare provider's office asks for it, usually with help from a support program.
A formal request asking your plan to reconsider a decision not to cover something. Plans usually have more than one level of appeal.
Your plan's list of covered drugs. A drug that isn't on the formulary may still be covered if the plan grants an exception.
The group a drug is placed in on the formulary. Higher tiers usually cost you more. Specialty medicines are often on the highest tier.
A plan rule that you try one or more other medicines first before the plan covers another.
The amount you pay for covered care each plan year before your plan starts to pay its share.
A fixed amount you pay for a covered medicine or service, such as a set dollar amount per fill.
Your share of the cost of a covered medicine or service, as a percentage of the price, after you've met your deductible.
The most you have to pay for covered care in a plan year. After you reach it, your plan pays 100% of covered costs for the rest of that year.
The part of the cost you pay yourself, whether as a deductible, copay or coinsurance.
A pharmacy that handles medicines needing special handling, monitoring or paperwork, and usually ships them to your home.
Permission from your plan to use a pharmacy outside the plan's usual rules, for example when the plan's required pharmacy can't supply a medicine.
A plan rule about how copay assistance counts. With some of these rules, money paid by a copay program doesn't count toward your deductible or out-of-pocket maximum.
A statement from your plan showing what it paid and what you owe. It isn't a bill.
The part of Medicare that covers prescription drugs, offered through private plans approved by Medicare.
A federal program that helps people with limited income and resources pay for Medicare drug coverage.
Income levels set each year by the federal government, by household size, and used to decide eligibility for many assistance programs.
